Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-30

Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Liam O'Reilly (Hawthorne Head of Platform), Sofia Martinez (Hawthorne SRE), Ethan Zhao (Hawthorne ML Infra)

Summary:
- Deep dive on autoscaling, burst policies, queueing behavior, and capacity planning for on-prem/VPC deployment.

Topics:

- Reserved capacity vs burst policies and pre-warming
- Queue models (FIFO priority, rate limiters, leaky bucket)
- KV cache behavior and cache warmup on scale-out
- Batching strategies and dynamic batching thresholds
- Quantization profiles impact on latency and throughput
- VPC/on-prem network constraints and cold-start implications

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining we wanted to spend this hour plus digging into your autoscaling and capacity planning for the private deployment, is that still the plan?
[00:12] Liam: yeah, thanks Jordan, appreciate it. we're trying to figure out how to size reserved GPUs and what burst behavior looks like when we do customer-facing inference, so like api traffic with spiky loads.
[00:24] Priya: great, quick intros from our side i'm priya, im the SE who works on runtime stuff, i'll own the benchmarking runbook with you.
[00:32] Sofia: hi all, sofia here, i'm the SRE, i'll be the day-to-day owner for autoscaling rules and ops.
[00:38] Ethan: ethan from ml infra, i'll share sample traces and the latency SLOs we care about.
[00:44] Jordan: perfect, so objectives for today: go over burst policies, queueing models, pre-warm strategies and how KV cache behaves when we scale out and back in.

[02:05] Priya: starting with the basics, our runtime supports several scaling triggers. you can drive scale with GPU utilization, active-inflight requests, or queue backlog thresholds. in practice for LLM inference we've found queue length + p95 latency to be the most stable since gpu util can be noisy with batching.
[02:28] Sofia: can you unpack that a bit? we run a mixed workload with short chat turns and some long generation jobs, how do you avoid one crowding out the other?
[02:40] Priya: yeah good question. we use prioritized queues and dynamic batching. short-turn requests get smaller batch windows and a higher priority lane so they cut ahead of long generations. we also have token-budgeting where longer jobs can be throttled if latency SLOs for the fast lane would be violated.

[04:15] Liam: what about burst capacity -- like when we get a marketing blast or sudden campaign, there are spikes 10x baseline for 5-10 minutes. do you recommend reserved GPUs or relying on burst?
[04:30] Jordan: depends on your predictability and cost tolerance. reserved GPUs give predictable tail latency and are great if you have a baseline. bursts are useful for short windows; we commonly recommend a hybrid: reserve enough for 70-80% baseline and configure a burst pool that can be pulled for short periods.
[04:52] Ethan: how does the burst pool connect? is it the same cluster or separate nodes that spin up? what's the cold start time?
[05:02] Priya: for private deployments we support two models: instant burst using pre-warmed standby instances in a burst pool, or on-demand spin-up which typically takes longer. pre-warmed nodes can be kept in a warm state with a tiny heartbeat to avoid full model load time; warm->ready typically 10-30s depending on model size and quantization. full cold start for a 70B non-quantized model can be multiple minutes.

[06:20] Sofia: that 10-30s number, is that realistic for our 33B model with 8-bit quantization?
[06:30] Priya: yes, with 8-bit quant and kernel cache warmed it's on the lower end; if you do int8 plus optimized kernels you're looking at sub-20s warm transitions. one caveat: KV cache warmup is separate. after a node becomes ready the KV cache is empty so first few requests will be slower until the prefix cache gets populated.
[07:05] Ethan: ok so KV cache warmup plus batch dynamics could cause a tail for the first minute or two. how do you model that in SLOs?
[07:15] Priya: we recommend a two-tier SLO: steady-state SLO and cold-warm SLO. steady-state p95 maybe 120ms for short turns; cold-warm p95 allowances for the 1-2min window where warmups happen. customers often set alerts on cache-hit rate and queue latency to detect when warmup is occurring.

[09:00] Jordan: moving on to queueing models, we support FIFO with weighted priorities, leaky-bucket token buckets for rate limiting, and a soft queue with overflow routing to a lower-cost model variant when latency is degrading.
[09:20] Liam: overflow routing sounds interesting, can you explain?
[09:26] Priya: sure. imagine you have a high-accuracy 33B model as your primary. when queue length exceeds a threshold or latency crosses SLO we route new requests to a 7B quantized variant or to a cached response when appropriate. that keeps external latency stable at the expense of some quality. routing policies are configurable per-route.

[11:40] Sofia: how about fairness across customers — if one customer spikes, can they consume the burst pool and starve others?
[11:50] Jordan: our burst pool enforces per-tenant burst caps and a credit model. you can assign reserved credits or per-tenant limits; excess requests are queued or routed to a best-effort pool. for Dedicated deployments we can also configure per-tenant GPU reservations.

[13:05] Ethan: can we see an example of the queue thresholds you recommend?
[13:12] Priya: typical config: baseline reserve for 70% of average qps, burst pool sized for 2-5x average for short windows, queue length threshold at 50-100 requests for prioritization rules, and dynamic batch cap so batches don't exceed 512 tokens. but it's very workload dependent.

[15:00] Liam: let's talk about batching. our current infra batches up to 8 requests with a 20ms batching window. is that similar?
[15:10] Priya: yeah similar. we use adaptive batching: batching window is tied to latency SLO and queue depth. if latency budget allows, window expands to increase throughput; if queues build, window shrinks. you can also set deterministic batching for latency-critical lanes.

[17:30] Sofia: do you support KV cache sharing across nodes? so if one node has seen a conversation prefix can another node reuse it?
[17:40] Priya: we do not share in-memory KV across distinct GPUs directly because of the memory copy cost; instead we have a distributed key-value store that stores compact prefixes and can warm a node quickly. it's eventual consistency and best-effort, so there's a short window where nodes will have different cache hit rates. this keeps memory footprint per GPU low while enabling fast warm paths.

[19:05] Ethan: sounds good. about quantization: we've seen some drop in quality moving to 4-bit. how do you recommend balancing throughput vs quality?
[19:16] Priya: we provide per-model quantization profiles. for many workloads 8-bit gives significant speedups with minimal quality loss. 4-bit is aggressive but can be acceptable for embedding-style workloads or reranking. we also suggest hybrid: use int4 for non-critical routes and int8 for customer-facing chat. we can run A/B evals with your prompt set to quantify regression.

[21:40] Jordan: from an ops perspective, what about monitoring and cost breakdowns?
[21:48] Priya: Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route latency, per-model resource usage, and cache hit metrics. crucially for capacity planning you can export a 24/7 heatmap of request arrival rates and tail latencies to drive reserved capacity sizing.

[23:05] Liam: ok let's outline a capacity plan. we want a pay-as-you-grow but with predictable tails for SLAs. what's your recommended initial reserved commit?
[23:18] Priya: we typically recommend reserving for 70-80% of 30-day rolling median peak traffic during business hours, then using burst pool sized to cover 90th-99th percentile short spikes. for on-prem you may want a higher reserve if you can't scale infra quickly.

[25:00] Sofia: is there a queuing model formula we can use to estimate required GPUs from request rates?
[25:08] Priya: yes, a rough formula: required_gpus = ceiling( (avg_tokens_per_second * avg_latency_seconds) / (tokens_per_second_per_gpu) ). tokens_per_second_per_gpu depends on model, quantization and batching. for planning we use bench numbers e.g., 33B int8 at steady-state 20k tokens/sec per A100-like GPU (example), but we'll run this with your traces.

[27:40] Ethan: can we get a sample benchmark run template? we'd like specific steps to reproduce locally.
[27:48] Priya: yes, i'll send a runbook. it includes: ingest traces, synthetic load replay, warmup procedure for KV prefix distribution, measuring p50/p95/p99 latency, measuring cache-hit progression, and failover tests for overflow routing.

[29:10] Liam: on the security side, since this is on-prem in our VPC, do you need network egress? how do upgrades work?
[29:22] Jordan: for Private deployments there's a customer-managed control plane option. minimal egress for metrics and licensing can be configured via proxy. upgrades are via controlled rollout with canary nodes and automatic rollback on regressions. we support KMS integrations and audit logs for compliance.

[31:05] Sofia: what's the expected operational overhead? we have a small infra team.
[31:12] Jordan: we offer a managed Private option with a support SLA and automated tooling; operational overhead depends on how much you want Redwood to manage. many customers run the control plane in their VPC but let Redwood handle model ops and core runtime updates with a support agreement.

[33:00] Ethan: regarding cost -- committed reserved GPUs vs burst usage billing -- how are burst minutes billed?
[33:12] Jordan: bursts are billed at a premium per-minute rate when you spin up on-demand. if you use pre-warmed standby nodes in the burst pool you pay a small keepalive fee for pre-warm capacity. dedicated reserved nodes are priced lower per-minute but require commit. we'll share a pricing sheet with examples.

[35:40] Priya: want to call out queueing backpressure strategies: aside from routing to smaller models, we also have adaptive rejection policies and client-side rate-limit hints. clients can be given a Retry-After with a soft token bucket so that retries are spread rather than causing thundering herd.

[37:05] Liam: do you expose those hints in the SDKs?
[37:10] Jordan: yes, our SDKs expose structured errors with retry metadata and suggested backoff. also metrics for estimated queue position.

[38:45] Sofia: is there a recommended approach to warm cache for scheduled events? we have daily digest runs that spike predictable loads.

[38:58] Priya: schedule pre-warm jobs that replay recent conversation prefixes into the KV store across the burst pool ahead of the event. pre-populating top-k prefixes reduces the initial tail. also keep a small number of warmed standby nodes specifically for scheduled spikes.

[41:20] Ethan: about measuring quality regressions when using lower-precision: what's the standard?

[41:28] Priya: we run prompt-based evals and A/B with held-out prompts. metrics include semantic similarity, end-task accuracy, and human-rated pass/fail thresholds. we can run those with your test set during the benchmark.

[43:00] Jordan: let's tie this to next steps and responsibilities.

[43:08] Priya: action item for me: draft the benchmark runbook and measurement sheet. i'll include warmup scripts and the overflow routing test.

[43:18] Jordan: action for me: send dedicated pricing and the security pack including SOC2 and network topology templates.

[43:25] Ethan: i'll export the sample traces and SLA doc.

[44:00] Liam: timeline wise we'd like to run the benchmark next week and have results by 2026-07-13. is that doable?

[44:10] Priya: yes, 48-72 hour benchmark starting whenever you can. i'll coordinate with sofia to ensure pre-warm windows.

[46:00] Sofia: one more ops question: if a node fails mid-conversation, do you rehydrate KV cache on failover? how does user experience look?

[46:10] Priya: we checkpoint KV deltas to a compact prefix store. failover will restart on another node which will gradually rehydrate. clients may see a slight drop in continuity for the first few tokens; we also support session-affinity to reduce cross-node disruptions.

[48:30] Jordan: any outstanding blockers?

[48:34] Liam: just clarifying pricing impact of pre-warmed standby nodes vs on-demand; we'll need numbers to make procurement decisions.

[48:45] Jordan: understood we'll include cost comparisons with example traffic profiles.

[50:00] Priya: last technical note: if you're using multi-tenant inference and want strict tenant isolation we recommend dedicated GPU pools per tenant; there's a tradeoff on efficiency but it gives no noisy neighbor risk and clearer capacity planning.

[52:20] Ethan: does Redwood support GPU heterogeneity? like mixing different instance types?

[52:28] Priya: yes, the runtime can schedule model variants based on available hardware; kernel selection and per-device optimization allow mixing but it complicates scheduling so we prefer homogeneous pools for strict SLOs.

[54:10] Sofia: any doc links you can share?

[54:14] Jordan: i'll upload the benchmark runbook and pricing examples to the deck, link: https://redwood.example.com/docs/private-benchmark-runbook (note link may be transcribed) and security pack at https://redwood.example.com/security/private-security-pack

[56:00] Liam: thanks, that helps a lot. we'll get the traces and confirm start time.

[56:08] Priya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the runbook and schedule.

[58:00] Jordan: quick recap: Priya will send runbook, Jordan will send pricing/security, Ethan provides traces, Sofia coordinates infra. follow-up week of 2026-07-14 to review benchmark.

[58:30] Liam: sounds good thanks all.

[60:00] Meeting end.
